body: In December 2004, The Weitz Company, LLC, general contractor on a multi-building retirement community in Shelby County, Tennessee, and Commercial Painting Company, Inc. entered into a drywall subcontract for $3,222,400, later raised by change orders to $3,315,189. Weitz paid 12 of Commercial Painting's 17 pay applications and refused the other five, saying they were untimely and contained improper change order requests. Commercial Painting sued Weitz and its sureties, Federal Insurance Company and St. Paul Fire & Marine Insurance Company, in Shelby County Chancery Court in August 2006, and Weitz counterclaimed for delay and defective work. Commercial Painting later added fraud and misrepresentation claims, alleging Weitz concealed a six-month extension it had negotiated with the project owner, which carried a bonus of $8,597 a day for up to 45 days of early completion, and then compressed the schedule, supplemented the drywall work and charged Commercial Painting for it.

In October 2018, a jury found for Commercial Painting on breach of contract, unjust enrichment, intentional misrepresentation and the payment bond, and the award totaled $8,359,863.83: $1,272,952.46 in compensatory damages, $2,083,362.16 in prejudgment interest, $1,103,549 in attorney's fees and $3.9 million in punitive damages. The trial court upheld the punitive award, finding that Weitz knew before signing that the project was about eight months behind, planned to compress the schedule and supplement the drywall work without telling Commercial Painting, and misrepresented the extension it later obtained. In 2022 the Court of Appeals reversed the punitive award under the economic loss doctrine. The Tennessee Supreme Court reversed that ruling in 2023 and, after a further appeal, directed the Court of Appeals in June 2025 to decide whether Commercial Painting had contractually waived punitive damages on its misrepresentation claim.

Judge Jeffrey Usman, joined by Judges J. Steven Stafford and Carma Dennis McGee, held that it had not. Section 11.6 of the subcontract bars anticipatory profit and indirect, special or consequential damages and waives "any other measure of damages" beyond those the subcontract provides, but it does not specifically waive damages for fraud or misrepresentation and appears to address contract remedies rather than tort. Under either the traditional view, reflected in Tennessee cases holding that "fraud vitiates all that it touches," or an approach that enforces only clear and specific waivers, the court concluded the clause does not bar the punitive award. It treated the jury's misrepresentation finding as the law of the case and held Weitz's ratification argument waived.
